content: The TB Alliance, formally known as the Global Alliance for TB Drug Development, is a non-profit organization focused on the discovery and development of new tuberculosis (TB) treatments that act faster, are more affordable, and are accessible to those in need. The organization aims to register a new anti-TB drug regimen by 2010 that could reduce the duration of TB treatment by one-third. In the long term, the TB Alliance seeks to develop a drug regimen that reduces the number of doses required for TB treatment from 130 to just 10. This regimen would also be effective against drug-resistant TB strains, compatible with antiretroviral drugs used for HIV treatment, and improve the management of latent TB infections. Tuberculosis currently infects one-third of the global population, causes two million deaths annually, and imposes a $16 billion economic burden on the global economy each year. Despite this, research and development for new TB drugs stagnated after the 1960s. The existing standard of care involves a combination therapy of four drugs, which requires six months or more to be effective. This prolonged treatment duration necessitates a level of monitoring that exceeds the capacity of healthcare systems in many countries. As a result, adequate TB treatment is available to less than half of the most infectious cases, which hampers disease control and contributes to the emergence of drug-resistant TB strains. Furthermore, TB is the leading cause of death among AIDS patients, yet current TB treatments are not well-suited for use alongside antiretroviral drugs for HIV. The TB drug market lacks sufficient financial incentives to encourage private pharmaceutical companies to invest in the research and development needed to sustain a robust treatment pipeline. The TB epidemic is concentrated in developing countries, where drugs must be low-cost to remain accessible. This economic reality does not generate the revenue streams that private companies typically require to justify the high costs and strategic risks associated with pharmaceutical research. The TB Alliance was established to address this gap and ensure that new anti-TB drugs are both affordable and accessible in countries where the disease is endemic. The TB Alliance was conceived during a meeting in February 2000 in Cape Town, South Africa, where 120 representatives from academia, industry, government agencies, non-governmental organizations, and donor groups convened to discuss the challenges of TB treatment. Participants emphasized the urgent need for faster-acting, novel TB drugs and highlighted the scientific opportunities available. The meeting culminated in the Declaration of Cape Town, which outlined a roadmap for TB drug development and called for the creation of the TB Alliance. The TB Alliance operates as a non-profit public-private partnership, functioning like a virtual biotechnology firm. It collaborates with research institutions and pharmaceutical companies to share risks and incentives while maintaining management oversight of its drug development projects. The organization outsources the development of potential drugs to public and private partners, providing funding and scientific guidance. Depending on the project, the TB Alliance may co-invest and co-develop, directly fund and manage, or in-license the technology or intellectual property involved. The Alliance prioritizes project diversity, selecting potential compounds from various chemical classes and targeting a wide range of mechanisms within the TB-causing organism, Mycobacterium tuberculosis. As of May 2006, the TB Alliance had 11 drug projects in development or undergoing human testing. A core part of the TB Alliance’s mission is to ensure that any new treatments are affordable and accessible in the developing world and that they are adopted as soon as they become available. Pricing terms are included in all licensing contracts, and the end products are designed to be user-friendly. The TB Alliance also collaborates with national and international partners to ensure that new therapies are adopted and made accessible to healthcare providers and patients through local distribution channels.
